You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel – Buyer-side review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Scope:** Seller's "Key Negotiated Positions" and Disclosure Letter dated 22 September 2026. This review is based on the Seller's own summaries; several points need checking against the full SPA drafting and the underlying DD documents before our mark-up goes out.

**Headline:** The package is not "fair and balanced." Taken together, the Seller's positions would (a) leave roughly AUD 4m+ of known, quantifiable liabilities sitting in the Company at Completion in what is meant to be a debt-free/cash-free deal, and (b) collapse the entire warranty and indemnity regime into a single 20%/18-month bucket that is further hollowed out by general disclosure and a constructive-knowledge exclusion. The known items alone (Riverlark AUD 3.2m, bonuses ~AUD 0.5m grossed up, Ironquay AUD 0.18m, Sandbar AUD 0.33m) approach the entire AUD 4.8m cap before any unknown warranty breach is considered.

---

## Part A – Economic / completion items (price-affecting)

### 1. Riverlark facility – AUD 3,200,000 (Clause 2 / 7)
**Seller position:** release "to be provided following Completion."
**Problem:** This is directly inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free price. If the facility is outstanding at Completion, we have paid AUD 24m for a company carrying AUD 3.2m of bank debt, and we are relying on an unsecured post-Completion promise from a seller that has just been paid out. DD-003 cl 8.1 (change of control) also suggests Completion itself is a default/review event — the bank could accelerate against *our* company on day one.
**Push back:**
- Repayment at Completion out of the purchase price via the funds flow (payoff letter from Riverlark specifying the discharge amount, delivered as a Completion deliverable).
- Executed deed of release and discharge of all security, PPSR release/discharge and any share mortgage release, delivered at Completion (not "following").
- Condition precedent or Completion deliverable for the Buyer's benefit; failing which price reduction equal to the payoff amount.
- Check PPSR now: if Riverlark holds security over the *shares* (not just Company assets), this is also a title issue (see item 14).

### 2. DD-005 completion bonuses – AUD 420,000 (Funds flow)
**Seller position:** "a matter for the Seller," not itemised.
**Problem:** These are triggered by Completion. They are a transaction cost of the Seller that crystallises as a liability of the Company we are buying. If the Seller genuinely accepts they are its cost, there is no reason not to itemise them. The disclosure itself admits that superannuation (SG at 12%), NSW payroll tax (~5.45%) and other on-costs are unaddressed — realistic grossed-up exposure is ~AUD 490k–500k. The "continued employment" condition also means part of the liability may fall post-Completion, when the Company (i.e., us) is the employer.
**Push back:**
- Define "Transaction Bonuses" (including all employer on-costs) and include them in Debt / as a deduction from the price, or have the Seller fund them at Completion through the funds flow with evidence of payment.
- Specific indemnity for any shortfall, including on-costs and any claim by the employees.
- Confirm the retention/continued-employment mechanics so we are not paying retention bonuses the Seller promised.

### 3. Ironquay – IP ownership gap (Clause 11.1)
**Seller position:** existing indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment (AUD 180k) is "adequate."
**Problem:** DD-004 cl 7.3 means the Company **does not own the SOW3 Project Materials** until every SOW3 fee is paid. DD-010 shows AUD 180k open. So a component of the product IP we are paying for currently belongs to a third-party developer. The exposure is not the AUD 180k; it is the loss of, or dispute over, IP embedded in the Company's product (and potentially in what is delivered to Bluefen). Under the Seller's cl 12.3 default, this indemnity would also be caught by the 20% cap and 18-month limit.
**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion obligation: Seller procures payment of AUD 180k (deducted from price / treated as Debt) **and** delivers a confirmatory IP assignment deed from Ironquay before Completion. Make this a CP or Completion deliverable.
- Broaden the indemnity to cover all loss arising from any defect in title to the Project Materials or any third-party claim, carved out of cap, basket and 18-month limit.
- Tighten IP warranties: the Company owns or validly licenses all IP in its products; no third party holds or is entitled to hold IP in them.

### 4. Sandbar supplier renewals – 3 × AUD 110,000 (DD-008 / DD-011)
**Seller position:** "ordinary-course operating costs."
**Problem:** The disclosure letter itself tells us to "read together for timing/scope" and expressly declines to say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. Three identical amounts totalling AUD 330k invite the question whether they were split to fall under an approval or materiality threshold, and whether they were entered during the exclusivity/conduct period.
**Push back:**
- Require full disclosure of the three contracts, counterparties (related-party check), dates, and whether they breached the pre-signing conduct-of-business covenants.
- If they are prepayments or commitments crystallising at/around Completion, treat as Debt-like or ensure the working capital peg captures them.
- Covenant that no further commitments above an agreed threshold are entered without Buyer consent.

### 5. Bluefen consent – ~30% of revenue (Clause 3 / 6.3)
**Seller position:** "reasonable endeavours"; consent treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.
**Problem:** DD-002 cl 11.2 requires consent *and* cl 11.3 imposes conditions. No consent exists. A bare written consent that leaves the 11.3 conditions unsatisfied, or that imposes new commercial terms (price concessions, termination rights), would technically "satisfy" the Seller's drafting while destroying the value of the contract. For a customer representing ~AUD 3.6m of revenue, "reasonable endeavours" is too weak.
**Push back:**
- CP for the Buyer's sole benefit (waivable only by the Buyer): unconditional written consent in a form approved by the Buyer, **plus** evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied, with no amendment to the Bluefen contract.
- "Best"/"all reasonable" endeavours plus Buyer right to participate in communications with Bluefen.
- Warranty that Bluefen has not indicated any intention to terminate, reduce volumes or renegotiate.
- Given concentration risk, consider a retention/escrow or earn-out component tied to Bluefen continuation through the first 12 months.

---

## Part B – Risk-allocation architecture (the warranty and indemnity regime)

### 6. General cap – 20% / AUD 4.8m (Clause 12.1)
20% is at the low end for an AUD 24m private M&A deal. More importantly, the Seller is trying to make it the *only* cap (see items 7–9). A 20% cap is only acceptable if it is confined to general warranties and we are comfortable with W&I insurance or a retention/escrow behind it.
**Push back:** Seek 30–50% for general warranties (or 20% with a 12–18 month escrow of a meaningful portion); 100% for fundamental/title, tax and specific indemnities.

### 7. Thresholds (Clause 12.2)
De minimis AUD 25k is tolerable; basket of AUD 250k (~1%) is market. Two problems: (a) it is a **deductible** ("only the excess"), not a tipping basket; (b) applied to "all Claims" it would bite on tax, title, leakage and specific indemnities.
**Push back:** Tipping basket (recover from the first dollar once exceeded); aggregate related claims for de minimis purposes; carve out fundamental warranties, tax, leakage and all specific indemnities.

### 8. Time limits and the "all Claims" default (Clause 12.3 / 13)
18 months is short (does not cover two audit cycles — 24 months is the normal buyer ask). The real issue is the sweep-up sentence: "any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise." This reverses the burden — anything we fail to carve out expressly is caught. It would subject the Ironquay indemnity, tax claims and title to 18 months and the 20% cap.
**Push back:**
- General warranties: 24 months.
- Tax warranties and tax indemnity: 7 years (ATO amendment periods plus a margin).
- Fundamental/title/capacity: at least 6–7 years, or no contractual limit.
- Specific indemnities: no time limit, or tied to the underlying statutory exposure.
- Delete the "applies to all Claims" default and replace with the reverse: limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly stated.

### 9. Fundamental and title warranties under the general cap
"Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap the Seller's liability for not owning what it is selling at 20%. If title fails, our loss is the whole price.
**Push back:** Title, capacity, authority and no-insolvency warranties capped at 100% of price, outside basket and de minimis, long survival. Non-negotiable.

### 10. Exclusive remedy / non-reliance to "all Claims of any nature" (Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
As drafted this would purport to exclude fraud, wilful concealment and dishonesty, and to cut off statutory claims. Note that an attempt to exclude misleading or deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law is of doubtful enforceability, but a broad non-reliance clause can still undermine such a claim, so the drafting matters.
**Push back:** Express carve-outs for fraud, dishonesty, wilful misconduct, wilful concealment, specific indemnities, leakage and claims under the Completion Accounts mechanism; non-reliance confined to pre-contractual representations not reflected in the SPA.

### 11. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (Schedule 7 / DL [1.1]–[1.2])
Blanket disclosure of "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room plus the Accounts, statutory registers and "publicly searchable corporate records" means any warranty is qualified by anything a diligent buyer *might* have found. Combined with cl 8.3 this makes the warranties close to worthless.
**Push back:**
- "Fairly disclosed" standard: disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and its likely impact.
- Public records limited to specified ASIC/PPSR/court searches against the Company conducted on a stated date, not open-ended.
- Specific disclosures only against the warranties they qualify.
- Disclosure Letter is dated 22 September 2026 and is now six weeks stale — require an updated letter at signing and a bring-down/no-new-disclosure confirmation at Completion, with Buyer walk right (or price adjustment) for material new disclosures.

### 12. Buyer knowledge exclusion (Clause 8.3)
"Knowledge … including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records" is a constructive-knowledge exclusion. It shifts the burden of the Seller's own disclosure quality onto us and turns every DD finding into a reason the Seller can refuse to pay.
**Push back:** Delete. If a knowledge qualification must be accepted, limit to **actual** knowledge of a short list of named Wattlebridge deal team members of the specific breach *and* that it constitutes a breach, and exclude specific indemnities (which exist precisely because we know of the issue).

### 13. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"
Not acceptable.
- **Tax:** Require a standard pre-Completion tax indemnity (all Tax of the Company referable to periods before Completion), 7-year survival, 100% cap, no basket. **Critical check:** is Paperbark a subsidiary member of a Harbourglass tax consolidated group? If so, we need a valid tax sharing agreement, a clear-exit payment and confirmation of exit before Completion, otherwise the Company remains jointly and severally liable for the whole group's income tax.
- **IP:** See Ironquay (item 3). Also warranties covering ownership of all product IP, employee/contractor assignment and moral rights consents, open-source compliance.

---

## Part C – Diligence-type items the disclosure letter flags but does not resolve

### 14. Title – share register only (DL [10])
The Seller is pointing at its own register and expressly disclaiming that we have verified anything. The register is not conclusive.
**Action:** ASIC company extract and historical extract, share certificates, constitution (pre-emption/transfer restrictions), PPSR search against Harbourglass for any security over the shares (Riverlark), confirmation of no options, convertibles or shareholder agreements. Warranty: Seller is legal and beneficial owner, shares fully paid, free of encumbrances, constitute 100% of issued capital.

### 15. DD-006 export / privacy incident (Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6)
~1,240 records of personal information sent to an unintended external recipient. The Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." The incident is known since at least 22 September; the 30-day assessment window under the Privacy Act Notifiable Data Breaches scheme has passed and the letter does not say the assessment was completed or what it concluded. Civil penalties for serious interferences with privacy now run into tens of millions of dollars, and if the data relates to Bluefen or other customers there may be contractual notification and indemnity obligations as well.
**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion: completed NDB assessment and copy of the report; evidence of any OAIC/individual/customer notifications made or a reasoned record of why not.
- Specific indemnity for all loss arising from the incident (regulatory penalties, remediation, customer claims and contractual liabilities, legal costs), outside cap/basket/time limits and not qualified by disclosure.
- Warranties on Privacy Act compliance and that there are no other unreported incidents.

### 16. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)
Lower risk but unresolved. For the lease, confirm the notification has actually been given or make it a Completion deliverable; check whether the "notification" clause also contains a landlord termination right. For Mossvale, obtain the actual clause — the Seller's characterisation ("does not state consent is required merely because shares are sold") is a legal conclusion we should verify, particularly for any change-of-control definition that captures ultimate ownership.

### 17. Disclosure Letter [1.4] and [11]
The non-admission language is standard, but read with the general-disclosure approach it means the Seller is disclosing everything while admitting nothing. [11] expressly puts the evaluative burden on us. That is fine so long as our warranty/indemnity package does the work; it is a reason to resist, not accept, the Seller's limitation regime.

---

## Summary of recommendations (in priority order)

| # | Issue | Our position |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Riverlark AUD 3.2m | Repay from funds flow at Completion; executed releases/PPSR discharge as Completion deliverables. Price reduction if not. |
| 2 | Bluefen consent (30% revenue) | Buyer-only CP: unconditional consent in agreed form + cl 11.3 conditions satisfied + no amendment. Consider escrow/earn-out. |
| 3 | Fundamental/title/tax carve-out | 100% cap, outside basket/de minimis, 6–7 yr (title) / 7 yr (tax); delete cl 12.3 "all Claims" default. |
| 4 | Completion bonuses AUD 420k + on-costs | Treat as Debt/price deduction, itemised in funds flow; specific indemnity. |
| 5 | Ironquay IP | Pay AUD 180k pre-Completion (deducted), confirmatory assignment as CP; broadened uncapped indemnity. |
| 6 | Privacy incident | Completed NDB assessment pre-Completion; specific indemnity outside limitations. |
| 7 | Clause 8.3 knowledge exclusion | Delete; at most actual knowledge of named individuals, excluding indemnities. |
| 8 | General disclosure | Fair-disclosure standard; specified searches only; updated DL at signing, bring-down at Completion. |
| 9 | Exclusive remedy / non-reliance | Carve out fraud, wilful misconduct, indemnities, leakage, Completion Accounts. |
| 10 | General cap / basket / time | Seek 30–50% or 20% with escrow; tipping basket; 24 months general. |
| 11 | Tax | Full pre-Completion tax indemnity; confirm tax consolidated group exit and clear-exit payment. |
| 12 | Sandbar renewals | Full disclosure of all three; conduct-of-business breach check; Debt-like or working capital treatment. |
| 13 | Title verification | ASIC, PPSR, certificates, constitution — our own searches, not the Seller's register. |
| 14 | Lease / Mossvale | Verify actual clauses; lease notice as Completion deliverable. |

**Suggested framing for the response to Harbourglass:** We are prepared to work within a conventional cap/basket/time-limit structure for *general* warranties, but only on the basis that (i) the known liabilities are settled through the price and funds flow in accordance with the agreed debt-free/cash-free basis, (ii) fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity claims sit outside those limitations, and (iii) the disclosure and knowledge provisions are brought back to market standard. Items 1, 2 and 3 in the table should be presented as pre-conditions to continuing, not negotiable trade-offs.

**Caveats:** This review relies on the Seller's summaries of its own clauses. Before the mark-up is finalised we should (a) read cl 12.3, 8.3, 9.3/12.8/20.5 and Schedule 7 in full, (b) pull DD-002, DD-003, DD-004 and DD-006 to verify the Seller's characterisations, and (c) run the ASIC/PPSR searches referred to at item 14. Consider also whether W&I insurance is available on this deal; if so, several of the cap/time-limit points can be solved through the policy rather than negotiation, but the known-issue items (1–6) will be excluded from cover and must be dealt with in the SPA.
=== END ADVICE ===
